synopsis: The existing warning fleet is the best available source of real off-road exposure, sensor recordings and false-alarm history: its logs can validate simulation inputs and submodels, but not the new closed-loop braking chain [f1252, f5122, f6611, f7575]. Collection should begin immediately, with fleet logging through winter 2026–2027, a searchable event corpus and exposure model; several early experiments can start in October 2026 [f708, f730, f10914]. Open-loop replay against independent ground truth establishes the warning-system baseline, while direct sensor-model reuse requires equivalent sensors and mounting, usable ground truth and coverage of relevant conditions; prototype sensor equivalence remains unknown [f94, f7930, f10891]. Three central traps limit inference: relevant-encounter exposure may be unknown, operator braking censors counterfactual outcomes, and warning history never exercised the detection-to-command-to-stopping chain; automatic braking also changes future human-system interaction [f12357, f7480]. Independent alarm evidence remains old and sparse: the cited 2006 NIOSH Caterpillar 793B study reported 18% false alarms and 42% nuisance alarms, and found the audible alarm switched off after shifts [f101, f102, f103, f104]. Despite its value, Chapter 6 did not consider this field-data source, no standard or assessor acceptance of legacy history as a simulator-validation reference was found, and the new braking target must come from its own hazard analysis rather than matching warning performance [f5121, f7580, f11989].
